{{Short description|Scottish cleric and mathematician}}
{{Use British English|date=August 2017}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=August 2017}}
'''William Braikenridge''' (also Brakenridge) ({{c.|1700–1762}}) was a Scottish mathematician and cleric, a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] from 1752.<ref>[http://royalsociety.org/DServe/dserve.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqCmd=Show.tcl&dsqDb=Persons&dsqPos=0&dsqSearch=%28%28text%29%3D%27Brakenridge%27%29 The Royal Society, ''Brakenridge; William (c 1700 – 1762)''.]</ref>

==Life==
He was son of John Braikenridge of [[Glasgow]].<ref name="Foster">[[s:Page:Alumni Oxoniensis (1715–1886) volume 1.djvu/169]]</ref> In the 1720s he taught mathematics in [[Edinburgh]].<ref>{{MacTutor|id=Braikenridge|title=William Braikenridge}}</ref>

Braikenridge was Honorary A.M. in 1735,<ref>Peter John Anderson (editor), ''Fasti Academiae Mariscallanae Aberdonensis: selections from the records of the Marischal College and University, MDXClll–MDCCCLX'' vol. 2 (1889) p. 308; [https://archive.org/stream/fastiacademiaema02univuoft#page/308/mode/2up  archive.org.]</ref> and D.D. in 1739, of [[Marischal College]], when he was vicar of New Church, [[Isle of Wight]].<ref>Peter John Anderson (editor), ''Fasti Academiae Mariscallanae Aberdonensis: selections from the records of the Marischal College and University, MDXClll–MDCCCLX'' vol. 2 (1889) p. 82; [https://archive.org/stream/fastiacademiaema02univuoft#page/82/mode/2up archive.org.]</ref> He was incorporated at [[The Queen's College, Oxford]], in 1741.<ref name="Foster"/> He became rector of [[St Michael Bassishaw]], and from 1745 librarian of [[Sion College]], in London.<ref>{{cite book|author=James Darling|title=Cyclopaedia Bibliographica: A Library Manual of Theological and General Literature, and Guide to Books for Authors, Preachers, Students, and Literary Men. Analytical, Bibliographical, and Biographical|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rNchAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA422|accessdate=2013-06-18|year=1854|publisher=s.n.|page=422}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Sion College and Library|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=I406AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA357|accessdate=2013-06-18|publisher=CUP Archive|page=357|id=GGKEY:ZARA8NG8R2Z|year=1913}}</ref>

==Works==
In geometry the [[Braikenridge–Maclaurin theorem]] was independently discovered by [[Colin Maclaurin]].<ref name="Cajori1991">{{cite book|author=Florian Cajori|title=A History of Mathematics|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mGJRjIC9fZgC&pg=PA228|accessdate=2013-06-18|year=1991|publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|isbn=978-0-8218-2102-2|page=228}}</ref> It occasioned a priority dispute after Braikenridge published it in 1733;<ref>{{cite book|author1=Colin MacLaurin|author2=Ian Tweddle|title=MacLaurin's Physical Dissertations|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iOHSw-TkK7MC&pg=PA3|accessdate=2013-06-18|date=1 January 2007|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-1-84628-776-3|page=3}}</ref> Stella Mills writes that, while Braikenridge may have wished to establish priority, Maclaurin rather felt slighted by the implication that he did not know theorems in the ''Exercitatio'' that he had taught for a number of years.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mills |first=Stella |date=1984 |title=Note on the Braikenridge-Maclaurin Theorem |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/531819 |journal=Notes and Records of the Royal Society of London |volume=38 |issue=2 |pages=235–240 |doi=10.1098/rsnr.1984.0014 |jstor=531819 |issn=0035-9149|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

[[File:Braikenridge.png|thumb]]
*''Exercitatio Geometrica de Descriptione Linearum Curvarum'' (1733)
*''Proposals for lectures on the principles of mechanicks and natural philosophy, by Mr. Braikenridge: Formerly teacher of the mathematicks at Edinburgh'' (1750?)<ref>[http://catalog.wrlc.org/cgi-bin/Pwebrecon.cgi?BBID=9405499 Catalogue page]</ref>
*''A Letter from the Reverend William Brakenridge, D.D. and F.R.S. to George Lewis Scot, Esq; F. R. S. concerning the Number of Inhabitants within the London Bills of Mortality (1 January 1753)'', in ''[[Philosophical Transactions]]''. This paper was topical, because parliament was considering legislation on a census and registration of vital information. Braikenridge argued, from [[bills of mortality]], that London's population had peaked a decade earlier; a controversy arose with Richard Forster of [[Great Shefford]]<ref>{{cite book|author=Andrea A. Rusnock|title=Vital Accounts: Quantifying Health and Population in Eighteenth-Century England and France|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GHQ8j0gqLuwC&pg=PA195|accessdate=2013-06-18|date=12 February 2009|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-10123-3|pages=195–7}}</ref> [[George Burrington]] also answered, in 1757.<ref>{{cite book|author=George Burrington|title=An answer to Dr. William Brakenridge's letter concerning the number of inhabitants, within the London Bills of Mortality: wherein the Doctor's letter is inserted at large, his arguments proved inconclusive, and the number of inhabitants increasing|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=j7ttugAACAAJ|accessdate=2013-06-18|year=1757|publisher=J. Scott}}</ref> It was argued against Braikenridge that population was increasing, near the area he considered.<ref>{{cite book|author=Paul Langford|title=A Polite and Commercial People: England, 1727–1783|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cy3hX944bLMC&pg=PA636|accessdate=2013-06-18|year=1992|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-285253-3|page=636}}</ref>
*'' A letter to the right honourable the earl of Macclesfield, president of the Royal society, concerning the method of constructing a table for the probabilities of life at London'' (1755)
*''A Letter to the Right Honourable Hugh Earl of Marchmont. F. R. S. concerning the Sections of a Solid, Hitherto Not Considered by Geometers; From William Brakenridge, D. D. Rector of St. Michael Bassishaw London, and F. R. S.'' (1759)
*''Sermons on Several Subjects by the Late William Brakenridge''<ref>{{cite book|author=William Brakenridge|title=Sermons on Several Subjects by the Late William Brakenridge|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ppBSbwAACAAJ|accessdate=2013-06-18|date=May 2010|publisher=BiblioBazaar|isbn=978-1-140-94108-8}}</ref> To which [[Jane Austen]]'s father, the Rev. George Austen subscribed whilst a fellow of St. John's College.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qCAHAAAAQAAJ&q=subscribers+austen&pg=PP9 | title=Sermons on several subjects| last1=Braikenridge| first1=William| year=1764}}</ref>
